statement:
Acts of Intelligence brings together 100 works from connected cultural collections to trace a longer history of agency: objects that see, measure, store, move, calculate, perform and appear to answer back.

This is not a narrow history of artificial intelligence. It is a cultural prehistory of agents. A telescope extends sight. An anatomical plate turns the body into a readable system. A praxinoscope, telephone, game, aircraft or control room delegates memory, judgement and action to a thing.

Every object can be opened and questioned through AUXIO. The replies are grounded in the object record, with the source institution, rights state and curatorial link kept visible.

sections.title: Seeing and Measuring
sections.intro: Instruments, images and systems that make the world observable. These works frame intelligence as a way of looking, measuring and converting distance into knowledge.
sections.question: What happens when an object teaches us how to see?

By converting visual data into tangible records, it underscores the exhibition’s theme of intelligence as a process of observation and measurement, laying groundwork for more sophisticated cognitive technologies.

works.title: Sky Study, Paris
works.medium: albumen print from wet collodion negative
works.description: This view frames the city so that the dome of the chapel of Les Invalides—a retirement home and hospital for military veterans—dominates the skyline. In the 1850s, the light-sensitive coatings for photographic plates were incapable of properly exposing both earth and the sky in a single shot. Marville here set his camera to capture the dramatic sky and clouds, which meant that the city below, for the most part, became a dark mass of undifferentiated buildings. The scale, drama, and majesty of this natural spectacle overwhelm human achievements.
works.curatorial_link: Charles Marville’s "Sky Study, Paris" captures the ephemeral beauty of clouds over the city, highlighting the technical challenge of balancing exposure between earth and sky in early photography. By prioritizing the atmospheric drama, Marville transforms his camera into an intelligent agent, one that selectively perceives and records, anticipating the computational decision-making inherent in later imaging technologies and AI systems.

works.institution: Museum of New Zealand Te Papa Tongarewa
works.description: This brass astronomical telescope is a Gregorian reflector type, made by Heath and Wing of London in about 1765. It uses two specially shaped metal mirrors to reflect light and create a magnified image, whereas earlier telescopes had used glass lenses to refract light. Gregory’s design resulted in smaller telescopes that produced sharper images, and was the forerunner of modern reflector telescopes. This telescope is associated with James Cook, an explorer who in 1768 was asked to command a long voyage to the Pacific to make astronomical observations. sections.title: Bodies as Systems
sections.intro: Anatomy, gesture, sensation and repair. Long before AI, collections treated the body as something that could be read, modelled, trained and extended.
sections.question: Where does intelligence sit between body, image and tool?

works.title: Hawkins Machine Model F automatic stamp franking machine
works.description: This Hawkins automatic stamp franking machine was the latest technology in the late 1920s, employing a gas meter-like system for stamping and franking business mail quickly and efficiently. It followed on from Moss franking machines which were at the leading edge of postal technology in the early 20th century. New Zealand engineer Ernest Moss invented 'Moss Machine No. 1' in about 1904, followed quickly by a series of innovative machines until the mid-1920s when C.R. Hawkins took over. This particular machine only has two impressions (1d and 2d), and was manufactured by The Automatic Franking Machine Company which had been founded by Messrs Moss and Dombrain.
works.curatorial_link: The Hawkins Machine Model F automatic stamp franking machine exemplifies early 20th-century technological innovation by automating a complex task through mechanical instruction, embodying the evolving concept of machine agency. As part of this lineage, it illustrates how devices like the Moss machines paved the way for more sophisticated systems that anticipate contemporary artificial intelligence through their embedded instructions and operational autonomy.

works.title: Printed Book of Hours (Use of Rome): fol. 95v, Text
works.artist: Guillaume Le Rouge (French, Paris, active 1493–1517); Master of the Très Petites Heures of Anne of Brittany…
works.description: Illustrated prayer books called books of hours remained popular with Europe’s elite well into the era of printing technology. This example belongs to a printed edition of five by the Parisian printer and engraver Guillaume Le Rouge, dating to 1510. Though printed on vellum (not paper), its 62 engraved pictures were hand-colored by an illuminator much like a traditional manuscript. By the mid-1480s, Paris was the center of production for books of hours with printed texts and engraved ornament. This book is therefore a hybrid fusing two distinct production methods—illumination and printing—representing the waning phase of the illuminator’s art prior to the complete transformation to printed books.
works.curatorial_link: This printed Book of Hours from 1510 exemplifies the transition in memory technologies during the Renaissance, blending mechanical printing with handcrafted illumination to produce a personalized prayer book. By integrating mechanized production techniques with human artistic intervention, it illustrates how memory was becoming both more standardized and customizable, foreshadowing later forms of agentive technology.

works.title: Red-Figure Column Krater (Mixing Vessel): Komos (Revel)
works.artist: Pig Painter (Greek, Attic, active c. 480–460 BCE)
works.description: Used for mixing wine and water at a symposium (drinking party), this vase bears images of komasts, or revelers, potentially mirroring the actions of its users. The three bearded men on side A stand out for their earrings, long drapery, and Eastern-style headdresses, and for the parasol held by one. Similar features have been noticed on numerous other red-figure vases, now called “Anakreontic” by scholars. This name refers to Anakreon, a 6th-century BC lyric poet from East Greece sometimes credited with inventing the barbitos, the long-stringed lyre played by the central figure on side A. The youths on side B, one draped, two nude and dancing, are less unusual.
works.curatorial_link: This krater from ancient Greece, used in symposiums where wine was mixed and consumed, features komasts who embody human revelry and social interaction, mirroring the drinkers' own behavior. The distinctive Eastern-style headdresses and parasol suggest a cultural hybridity that anticipates later notions of artificial agency as entities that blend and reflect diverse human attributes and perspectives.

works.artist: Antimenes Painter (Greek, Attic, active c. 530–510 BCE)
works.description: Comparison with better-preserved vases—and with other artworks and monuments, such as the famous Siphnian Treasury at Delphi—helps to fill in some of the action no longer surviving from the rest of this vase, which once showed Apollo and Herakles struggling for the Delphic tripod. One claw-footed leg of the tripod survives, across the chest of Zeus, the bearded figure who intervened to stop the quarrel between two of his sons. Apollo is the unbearded figure at left, while Herakles would have appeared beyond the break on the right.
works.curatorial_link: This fragment from a Black-Figure Neck-Amphora depicts Apollo and Zeus, capturing a moment where divine figures interact with an emblematic tripod, symbolizing wisdom and prophecy. The partial representation of the tripod and the intervention by Zeus reflect ancient narratives that imbue objects with agency and significance, echoing the exhibition’s exploration of how matter is endowed with intelligence and perspective across cultural histories.

works.description: This round-bodied oil vessel, produced in Paestum, belongs to a small group of vessels decorated with black figure in the second half of the fourth century BC, long after the technique had previously fallen out of fashion. Unlike most such vessels, which are smaller and feature just a single figure (often a woman or bird), this one shows a more complex and colorful scene. The goat-legged god Pan perches on a branched tree trunk, holding his syrinx (panpipe) and a hare. Facing him, her hands on the trunk, is a draped woman, perhaps a nymph or the moon goddess Selene.
works.curatorial_link: This lekythos, with its intricate black-figure depiction of Pan presenting a hare to a woman, exemplifies ancient Greece’s anthropomorphized deities and creatures, reflecting a human tendency to imbue matter with life and intelligence. By attributing agency even to mythic beings like Pan, the vessel foreshadows modern practices that animate objects and machines in our quest for intelligent agents.

works.description: There is a collection of 12 engraved profile portraits arranged in a grid. Each portrait shows a person from the chest upwards, in a circular frame. The individuals are depicted in side profile, facing left or right, wearing formal attire common in the late 18th to early 19th century. The portraits vary in facial features, hair styles, and clothing. Each portrait is labeled with a name in cursive script, including names like Danl Ludlow, Wm Barney, Brunnel, and others. The background is a plain beige mounting board, contrasting with the dark circular backgrounds behind each portrait.

works.curatorial_link: The Saint-Mémin Collection of Portraits presents meticulously crafted profiles that epitomize early efforts to capture human likeness with mechanical precision, reflecting an era when technology began to mirror human attributes. By arranging these portraits as designed characters with discernible personalities and social roles, Saint-Mémin underscores the enduring human impulse to imbue matter with agency and a subjective presence.

works.title: Bwoom Mask
works.description: A mask from the Kuba Kingdom . Kuba mythology revolves around three figures, each represented by a masquerade character: Woot, the creator and founder of the ruling dynasty; Woot’s spouse; and Bwoom. Bwoom’s specific identity varies according to different versions of the myth. He may represent the king’s younger brother, a person of Twa descent, or a commoner. Embodying a subversive force within the royal court, the Bwoom masquerade is often performed in conflict with the masked figure representing Woot.
works.curatorial_link: The Bwoom Mask from the Kuba Kingdom embodies a complex figure in mythology who challenges authority, representing subversive forces within the royal court. By taking on human and sometimes non-elite forms, this mask exemplifies how cultural artifacts can animate matter with agency, foreshadowing contemporary notions of intelligent, autonomous objects.

works.title: Portret van Karel de Stoute, hertog van Bourgondië
works.description: Portret van Karel de Stoute, hertog van Bourgondië, staande naar links in een harnas met op zijn schouder een wapenschild en in zijn hand, over zijn andere schouder, een zwaard. Prent uit een serie van 36 prenten met portretten ten voeten uit van graven en gravinnen van Holland.
works.curatorial_link: Adriaen Matham’s etching portrays Charles the Bold, Duke of Burgundy, in intricate detail, embodying the portrait as a vessel for storing historical and cultural memory—a role traditionally reserved for human intelligence. By depicting a figure with such authority, this work suggests how objects can assume agency through their representation, foreshadowing modern concepts where machines store, process, and convey vast repositories of knowledge and identity.

works.title: Portret van Robrecht I de Fries, graaf van Vlaanderen
works.description: Portret van Robrecht I de Fries, graaf van Vlaanderen, tweede echtgenoot van Geertruid van Saksen, staande in een harnas met op zijn schouder een wapenschild en in zijn hand een zwaard. Prent uit een serie van 36 prenten met portretten ten voeten uit van graven en gravinnen van Holland.
works.curatorial_link: Adriaen Matham’s portrait of Robrecht I de Fries, Count of Flanders, rendered in intricate detail with armor and weapons, exemplifies the human tendency to imbue figures of power with a commanding presence that borders on the animate. This meticulously crafted image resonates within the exhibition’s exploration of agency, suggesting how even static representations can be perceived as agents with their own histories and roles.

works.title: Three faced doll
works.institution: Museum of New Zealand Te Papa Tongarewa
works.medium: ceramic, metal, paper, wood, papier-mâché, straw, horsehair, kapok, gesso, plaster, string, glass,…
works.description: This is a rare three-faced mechanical doll, made about 1900 by the renowned Gebruder Heubach firm in Germany. Design By means of a ring and rod device, the head may be turned within its protective hood to reveal a crying, sleeping or smiling face. The doll has a voice box mechanism operated by a pull-string that emerges from its hip. The doll is wearing a simple white cotton shift, fine white muslin drawers, and a long-waisted, white, machine-embroidered dress. It would have originally worn a bonnet over the papier-mâché hood. works.curatorial_link: This rare three-faced mechanical doll by Gebruder Heubach exemplifies the early 20th-century fascination with imbuing objects with human-like characteristics, as each face—crying, sleeping, or smiling—responds to manual manipulation, reflecting an era when mechanical devices were designed to mimic emotional states and engage viewers on a personal level. The doll’s voice box mechanism further underscores its role in the cultural prehistory of AI by embodying the aspiration to create interactive agents that appear sentient and responsive.

works.title: Portret van Arnulf, graaf van Holland
works.description: Portret van Arnulf, graaf van Holland, staande naar links in een harnas met op zijn schouder het wapen van Holland en over zijn andere schouder een zwaard. Prent uit een serie van 36 prenten met portretten ten voeten uit van graven en gravinnen van Holland.
works.curatorial_link: Adriaen Matham’s etching “Portret van Arnulf, graaf van Holland” portrays a noble figure clad in armor with Holland’s coat of arms, embodying the historical personification of authority and power through visual representation. This portrait contributes to the exhibition's exploration by illustrating how human attributes are ascribed to figures rendered in art, foreshadowing contemporary tendencies to imbue machines and AI with agency and identity.

works.title: Portret van Godfried III met de Bult, hertog van Neder-Lotharingen
works.description: Portret van Godfried III met de Bult, hertog van Neder-Lotharingen, staande naar links in een harnas met op zijn schouder een wapenschild en in zijn hand een speer. Prent uit een serie van 36 prenten met portretten ten voeten uit van graven en gravinnen van Holland.
works.curatorial_link: Adriaen Matham’s etching portrays Godfried III, Duke of Lower Lorraine, standing resolutely in armor, his presence imbued with the authority befitting a noble figure. This portrait exemplifies how human art has long endowed figures with an almost autonomous agency, anticipating the cultural tendency to animate and attribute intelligence to mechanical and digital entities.

works.title: Portret van Dirk VII, graaf van Holland
works.description: Portret van Dirk VII, graaf van Holland, staande in een harnas met op zijn schouder het wapen van Holland en in zijn hand een zwaard. Prent uit een serie van 36 prenten met portretten ten voeten uit van graven en gravinnen van Holland.
works.curatorial_link: Adriaen Matham’s standing portrait of Dirk VII, Count of Holland, rendered in armor with the coat of arms of Holland on his shoulder and a sword in hand, exemplifies how portraiture bestows agency by imbuing static figures with presence and authority. This detailed engraving participates in the room’s inquiry into why humans anthropomorphize objects, here elevating a historical figure to an almost autonomous agent through the power of visual representation.
